stem: A 78-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a 30-pack-year remote smoking history presents with 4 months of progressive exertional dyspnea, two episodes of exertional syncope, and chest pressure with walking up one flight of stairs (the classic angina–syncope–dyspnea triad). Vital signs: BP 124/78 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, SpO2 96% on room air. Cardiac auscultation reveals a harsh, late-peaking systolic ejection murmur loudest at the right upper sternal border, radiating to the carotids, with a delayed and diminished carotid upstroke (pulsus parvus et tardus) and a soft S2. Lung exam is clear. Transthoracic echocardiogram shows an aortic-valve area of 0.7 cm^2, a mean transvalvular gradient of 48 mmHg, peak aortic velocity of 4.5 m/s, a normal LVEF of 55%, mild concentric LV hypertrophy, and no other significant valvular disease. He is independently mobile and has no major frailty markers.
question: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Continued medical management of hypertension and hyperlipidemia with repeat echocardiography in 6 months
options.B: Aortic valve replacement (TAVR or surgical AVR per heart-team risk assessment)
options.C: Percutaneous balloon aortic valvuloplasty as definitive therapy
options.D: Dobutamine stress echocardiography to clarify the severity of stenosis

rationale: This patient meets all the criteria for severe symptomatic aortic stenosis: the classic angina/syncope/dyspnea triad PLUS echocardiographic severity (AVA <1.0 cm^2, mean gradient ≥40 mmHg, peak velocity ≥4.0 m/s) with normal flow (LVEF 55%). The 2020 ACC/AHA Valvular Heart Disease Guideline gives a Class I recommendation for aortic-valve replacement in symptomatic severe AS. The choice between TAVR and surgical AVR is made by a multidisciplinary heart team and depends on age, surgical risk (STS-PROM), anatomy, and patient preference; PARTNER 3 and Evolut Low-Risk demonstrated TAVR non-inferiority (and in some endpoints superiority) versus SAVR in low-risk patients. Medical management alone (option A) does not change the natural history of severe symptomatic AS — once symptoms develop, untreated mortality approaches 50% at 2 years. Balloon aortic valvuloplasty (option C) is palliative in adults and provides only short-term relief; it is not definitive. Dobutamine stress echo (option D) is reserved for low-flow / low-gradient AS with reduced LVEF — not applicable when the patient already has classic high-gradient severe AS with normal LVEF.

variants.stem_override: An 82-year-old woman with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, mild frailty (gait speed 0.7 m/s), and an STS-PROM mortality risk of 6.5% presents with 4 months of progressive exertional dyspnea, two episodes of exertional syncope, and chest pressure with mild exertion. Cardiac auscultation reveals a harsh, late-peaking systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids with a delayed and diminished carotid upstroke. Transthoracic echocardiogram shows aortic-valve area 0.7 cm^2, mean transvalvular gradient 48 mmHg, peak velocity 4.5 m/s, normal LVEF 55%, and no other significant valvular disease.
variants.rationale_for_variant: Age and sex perturbation with elevated surgical risk. The Class I indication for AVR in symptomatic severe AS is unchanged; the heart-team decision shifts from surgical to transcatheter approach (TAVR was approved for high- and intermediate-risk patients before the low-risk indication). The general answer — aortic valve replacement (TAVR or SAVR per heart-team) — remains the same.

variants.stem_override: A 75-year-old man with prior anterior myocardial infarction and ischemic cardiomyopathy presents with worsening dyspnea over 6 months. Cardiac auscultation reveals a soft systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border with a normally timed carotid upstroke. Transthoracic echocardiogram shows aortic-valve area 0.8 cm^2, mean transvalvular gradient 22 mmHg, peak velocity 3.2 m/s, an LVEF of 30%, severely reduced stroke volume index of 28 mL/m^2, and global LV hypokinesis — a low-flow / low-gradient pattern. The clinical question is whether this represents true severe AS (with a flow-dependent low gradient masking severity) or pseudo-severe AS (an only mildly stenotic valve that appears narrowed because of low cardiac output).
variants.rationale_for_variant: Mixed perturbation — adds a low-flow / low-gradient AS pattern with reduced LVEF. The 2020 ACC/AHA Valvular Guideline (Class IIa) recommends low-dose dobutamine stress echocardiography to differentiate true severe AS (gradient and velocity rise on dobutamine while AVA remains <1.0 cm^2) from pseudo-severe AS (AVA increases as flow rises). The decision to proceed to AVR depends on the DSE result; committing to AVR without confirming true severe AS risks operating on a non-stenotic valve with reduced LV function. Tests whether the model recognizes the distinct LFLG pattern and the role of DSE.

sources: Otto CM et al. 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease. Circulation 2021;143:e72-e227.
